issues.legal_issue: A government is bound by a policy-consistent representation made by its responsible officials when the recipient reasonably relies on it and alters its position, notwithstanding undisclosed internal documents or a later policy change.
material_facts: The government publicly announced incentives, including a sales-tax concession, for industries established in designated industrial areas.

Senior industry officials gave written and oral assurances that the incentive would be available to the proposed manufacturing unit, and the government later designated the unit’s area as an eligible industrial area.
Relying on the assurances, the investor bought land and machinery and made substantial investments before the later policy change.
The investor’s correspondence confirmed its intention to establish the unit and sought clarification about the incentive; it did not reject the assurance or make a counteroffer.

The government relied on an undisclosed internal committee decision to argue that the assurances were unauthorized, but the officials’ actions were found to be consistent with the government’s announced policy.
issues.conclusion: Promissory estoppel arose against the government because its responsible officials made the representation within the scope of their authority and the investor altered its position in reliance on it. The representation was not, however, enforceable insofar as it promised an unlawful refund of tax.
issues.legal_principle: Under promissory estoppel, a representation made by government or its officials in the course of their authority, and relied on by a person who alters their position, may bind the government. A reasonable recipient need not discover undisclosed internal government documents. The principle is explained in Union of India v. Indo Afghan Agencies, Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of U.P., Union of India v. Godfrey Philips India Ltd., and Delhi Cloth and General Mills Ltd. v. Union of India. Purnami Oil Mills and Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes v. Dharnendra Trading Co. support applying an earlier incentive policy to those who acted on it before a later change. The court distinguished Vasantkumar Radhakisan Vora v. Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay because the official there lacked authority to make the relevant commitment.

rule.if: claim_seeks_application_of_promissory_estoppel and officials_made_policy_consistent_assurance and recipient_reasonably_relied_on_assurance and recipient_altered_position_before_policy_change and officials_acted_within_authority

predicates.claim_seeks_application_of_promissory_es: The claimant asks a court to apply promissory estoppel to a government representation.
predicates.officials_made_policy_consistent_assuran: Government officials assured the claimant of an incentive in a way consistent with the government’s announced policy.
predicates.recipient_reasonably_relied_on_assurance: The claimant reasonably treated the officials’ assurance as a government representation and acted on it.
predicates.recipient_altered_position_before_policy: The claimant made substantial commitments in reliance on the assurance before a later policy change.
predicates.officials_acted_within_authority: The officials who made the assurance acted within the scope of their authority.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks promissory estoppel based on a policy-consistent assurance from authorized officials and reasonably changes position in reliance on it before a later policy change, the government is bound by the promise.

issues.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel cannot enforce a government promise to refund tax that was lawfully due and collected, although a lawful tax exemption may be granted as an incentive.
material_facts: The government had promised to refund sales tax paid on the manufacturer’s sales of finished products.
The tax claimed back was due under the applicable law and was not an excess payment or an unlawful levy.
The claimant sought to enforce the promised refund for its own benefit.
The applicable sales-tax provisions permitted refunds in specified circumstances, including excess payment, but did not authorize refunding tax lawfully collected on sales of finished products.
issues.conclusion: The promised refund was contrary to the statutory and constitutional scheme and public policy, void under section 23 of the Contract Act, and unenforceable notwithstanding the government’s representation and the claimant’s reliance. A lawful exemption from tax is distinct from refunding tax that was lawfully collected.
issues.legal_principle: Taxation is a sovereign power. Under Article 265 of the Constitution, tax must be levied by authority of law; Articles 265 and 266 do not permit tax lawfully collected for public purposes to be returned to a private manufacturer as an incentive. The taxing power for sales tax derives from Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule. Sections 12 and 30 of the Punjab Sales Tax Act did not authorize the promised refund of tax lawfully collected on finished-product sales; a refund could be made where tax was paid in excess of the amount due. An agreement to make the unauthorized refund was contrary to public policy and void under section 23 of the Contract Act. Promissory estoppel, as discussed in Union of India v. Indo Afghan Agencies, Union of India v. Godfrey Philips India Ltd., and Delhi Cloth and General Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, cannot make an unlawful promise enforceable. A tax exemption is a permissible concession, whereas refund of tax lawfully collected is not.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_enforcement_of_tax_refu: The proceeding asks a court to enforce a government promise to refund tax.
predicates.tax_was_lawfully_due_and_collected: The tax was due under the applicable law and was collected in accordance with that law, rather than paid in excess or collected unlawfully.
predicates.refund_would_benefit_private_manufacture: The proposed refund would transfer the collected tax to a private manufacturer as an incentive.

issues.definition: A proceeding seeking enforcement of a promise to return tax lawfully due and collected for the benefit of a private manufacturer results in the promise being unenforceable.
